item.title: The Benefits of Replacing Control With Curiosity
item.description:
Family Dynamics

The Benefits of Replacing Control With Curiosity

How parents can reconnect with adult children by learning to listen, not judge.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Parents must try to understand rather than dictate their adult children's choices.
  • Parents may mistakenly assume that what was beneficial for them must also be beneficial for their children.
  • A parent's fear of losing influence over an adult child can inadvertently drive that child away.
Source: RoonzNL/Pixabay

In my previous post, I discussed the common origins of estrangement between parent and adult child during the emptying of the family nest.

I shared the story of Robert, who, you may recall, was angry with his son, Andrew, for not continuing to follow the religious pathway that he had so carefully laid out for him. Rather than being interested in Andrew’s personal evolution as he approached college graduation, Robert became critical and judgmental, which was pushing his son away at a critical developmental juncture.

Robert came to consult with me to discuss how to bring Andrew “back into the fold,” which, from his perspective, appeared to mean convincing his son to return to the conventional Christian journey that Andrew had dutifully been traveling since he was a child.

But for Robert to have any success repairing the gash that had opened up in the father-son relationship, he would need to take a look at his own reactivity to Andrew’s autonomy.

Here's a segment from our initial consultation:

R: I just don’t understand what happened. He was so involved in the church, so involved in the campus ministry, and now he’s not doing any of that. He was planning on doing a year of mission work in Ghana after he graduated, and now he told us that he’s not planning on that, either.

Dr. S: Do you know what he’s thinking about doing as an alternative?

R: No, I don’t. That’s one of the problems. It’s like pulling teeth with him right now. He hasn’t said much of anything. He never picks up the phone when my wife and I call, and when he does, he just gives one-word answers.

Dr. S: I understand that there was a blowup when he was home on spring break?

R: Yeah, he didn’t want to go to church with the family. That’s simply not acceptable. There’s no excuse for that. He’s part of the family; he should act like part of the family. After all, I’m paying for his college, you know.

Dr. S: Did you take any time to ask him why he didn’t want to go to church?

R: Why should I? I’m not interested in his reasons for not going; I’m interested in his going—like he always did, like he should do, like everyone else in the family does.

Dr. S: Perhaps that’s part of why he didn’t want to go. Perhaps he wants to strike out on his own, feel a little bit “apart” from the family rather than always feeling like “a part" of the family.

R: I’m all for striking out on your own, but he’s still a part of the family.

Dr. S: Of course he is, and he always will be. But part of his job right now as a young man is becoming his own man, and finding his own way of moving through the world, while still being part of the family.

R: He can be his own man and still go to church, can’t he?

Dr. S: Of course he can. But right now he may be feeling like he needs the opportunity to make decisions independently to see how it feels…and to see how those decisions turn out.

R: Oh, he’ll find out, alright. You can see what’s happening in the world right now as people turn away from religion. It’s a disaster out there.

Dr. S: But we don’t know that he’s turning away from religion. Right now, all we know is that he’s turning away from the form of religious observance that he was raised with, and that he initially planned on following. It doesn’t sound like you know too much about his spiritual life at this point.

R: He won’t tell me!

Dr. S: Have you asked?

R: (silence)

Dr. S: Could you ask?

R: (after some additional silence) I could. But I’m afraid to find out what he’d have to say. I’m afraid I’d hear that he’s giving up on religion.

Dr. S: But unless you ask, you won’t know. And unless you ask, he may conclude that you don’t have any interest in him and his life unless he’s expressing religious commitment and spiritual devotion according to your definition of them.

R: I might not be happy with what he has to say.

Dr. S: You might not. But he is probably not very happy that he doesn’t feel free to talk to his own father about what he’s thinking and what he’s feeling without being told that he’s being unappreciative and disrespectful. Which may be why he’s pulling away from you.

R: He knows I’m here to talk anytime!

Dr. S: But does he know that you’re here to listen?

It was natural for Robert to want Andrew to continue to cultivate the religious identity that he, as a father, had done, and that he had in mind for his son.

A subsequent session with Robert revealed that he was the youngest of five children, both of his parents worked full-time jobs to make ends meet, and there simply wasn’t much attention paid to him. But he recalled for me how religious school, and the youth minister at his neighborhood church, had supplied him with the emotional resources that his family had been unable to provide. So it was natural for Robert to insist that Andrew travel the fruitful trail that he had been traveling. But it was just as natural for Andrew to push back and find a trail to travel that felt like his own, one that might or might not turn out to mirror his father’s.

Nevertheless, as a result of our consultations, Robert softened his stance and displayed less fear and more curiosity regarding Andrew’s journey. Unsurprisingly, their relationship began to soften as well, and the continued estrangement that they had been veering toward began to feel less inevitable as they figured out how to connect as two adults rather than as a controlling parent and a deferential child.

item.title: Real or Not? Teaching Children About Generative AI
item.description:
Parenting

Real or Not? Teaching Children About Generative AI

Practical advice on teaching children about generative AI.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • In our study, children who knew about AI identified more videos correctly.
  • Children identified AI videos better than chance, but fewer than half identified every video correctly.
  • Children often judged whether a video seemed possible; few noticed AI labels.
  • Parents can teach children to question implausible scenes and look for visual or audio inconsistencies.

This post was coauthored by Lydia Rowley, a student at Brigham Young University.

Imagine this: You unlock your phone and open Instagram. The first post you see is a video of a popular public figure making rude, racist comments. You’re stunned. You never thought they would endorse those viewpoints. As your finger hovers over the unfollow button, you watch the video again—and notice a few little details that change everything. The hair and skin are a little too shiny. The motions are too smooth. A few people in the background disappear between shots. Clicking on the comments confirms your suspicions: This video is AI-generated.

You close Instagram, relieved to realize the truth. But the fear lingers: Would you notice next time? Even more concerning, would your children notice?

Visual Deception

Generative AI becomes more realistic with every update, making it ever more difficult to differentiate AI-generated from real content. Some studies claim children cannot differentiate AI from real content as well as adults, who are not particularly successful themselves. However, new data from our under-review paper shows that 9-year-old children did better than guessing when asked to identify AI-generated videos, though less than half (46.5 percent) identified all the videos correctly. Children’s understanding of AI is related to their ability to identify it. The 54.7 percent of children in our study who said they knew what AI was correctly identified more videos than their less familiar peers.

Parents are often a child’s first source of information, so in-home education about AI-generated content is essential. But what do we teach children about how to identify this new technology? In our research, currently under review, children most readily identified an AI-generated video involving babies riding animals in a fashion show, explaining that this could never happen in real life. Some children noticed when the AI made errors with lighting, skin, or hair, but surprisingly few made note of a caption stating that the video was AI-generated. These observations show us what we can do to help children learn to identify AI-generated videos.

Teaching Children to Identify AI

How can we teach children to identify AI-generated videos? The following suggestions build on our findings.

  1. Start early. The children in our study were 8 and 9 years old, but most understood our explanation of AI, and many were already familiar with it. While relatively few could give an accurate definition, children of this age are ready to learn about AI and can understand what it is and what it does.
  2. Be concise and use examples. Children can understand what AI is, but they are more likely to retain and understand a simple, age-appropriate definition with relevant examples. For instance, parents could explain that AI is a computer that is programmed to think and learn like a person. Parents can share that AI is made to answer questions, solve problems, recognize patterns, and generate text, images, audio, and videos. Relevant examples of AI include Siri, Google, Alexa, Netflix’s recommendation system, and chatbots like ChatGPT. Including the names of specific image generators (Sora, Seedance, etc.) and the logos associated with them can help children notice and understand the watermarks that appear on many AI-generated images and videos.
  3. Start with a reality check. The most common reason children gave for saying a video was AI-generated was that it couldn’t happen in real life, so encouraging a reality check is a good place to start. Prompt your children to consider if the content could occur in real life, or if the content looks, sounds, or behaves like it should in real life. Be sure to address the difference between acting in a movie, which is not real life but is done by real people, and AI-generated videos.
  4. Talk about “tells.” Some children identified specific AI-related digital artifacts, or “tells,” in the videos. Pointing these out helps children know what to look for in the future, so instruct children to look for "tells" like nonsense words, anatomy problems, odd lighting, blurriness, oddly smooth surfaces, mismatch between voices and mouth movements, and inconsistency in objects, background, or motion.

Conclusion

As AI-generated videos and images become increasingly common on the internet, parents can prepare their children to thoughtfully and critically evaluate this content. By educating children with age-appropriate definitions and relevant examples, discussing the implausibility of some AI-generated content, and explaining specific “tells” to look for while evaluating online content, parents can help children develop the critical thinking skills necessary to differentiate real and AI-generated content. AI-generated content is not going away anytime soon, but by educating their children, parents don’t need to be quite so afraid of its deception.

item.title: Social Media Shaming: A Life Reduced to One Moment
item.description:
Social Media

Social Media Shaming: A Life Reduced to One Moment

The psychological forces behind online pile-ons.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • We tend to blame the mistakes of others on character while excusing our own as the result of circumstances.
  • Negative impressions carry more psychological weight than positive ones and are slower to change.
  • In a post, each additional morally charged emotional word increases its spread by approximately 20%.
  • Research finds online harassment in adults is linked to depression, anxiety, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts.

In today’s world, we are reduced and judged by one word, one action.

We can spend our entire lives being good people raising children, showing up for friends, helping strangers, and building our work and our reputations slowly, one honest interaction at a time. Then a single word, typed carelessly or while driving or said in the wrong moment, becomes the only thing people see.

And, it often begins with a post when someone is upset, and instead of reaching out, they go to social media. Then others chime in, people who have literally never met the person and know nothing about their life or their history. Within hours, strangers have decided what that person believes, what they value, and who they are. And it doesn’t end there; Employers get tagged, and sometimes businesses or friends get named. And before you know it, a reputation built over decades can begin to unravel over a sentence, often before anyone has asked a single question or verified a single detail. Not to mention that much of the time what people hear when they read might be perceived incorrectly.

People should be responsible for what they say, and sometimes what they say does real harm or you don’t agree with. What concerns me is how quickly we’ve come to believe that one moment tells us everything about a person, as though nothing else they ever did or said counts.

Why Our Minds Go There So Fast

Psychologists have studied this tendency, the fundamental attribution error, for decades (Lee Ross, 1977). We explain other people’s behavior through their character and our own through our circumstances. Sometimes if I poorly word something or it comes out wrong, I know I was tired or distracted or maybe even just chose the wrong word. When you say something that might be poorly worded, I’m far more likely to decide it reveals who you really are.

Once that impression forms, confirmation bias reinforces it. We pay attention to what supports our first read or impression of someone and overlook what challenges it (Nickerson, 1998). In addition, we are sensitive to the negative. Decades of reviewed research shows that bad experiences and impressions carry more psychological weight than good ones (Baumeister et al, 2001). Someone can spend years doing good, and one offensive comment becomes the thing people remember. Of course the offensive comment matters, but so does the rest of that person’s life.

What Social Media Adds

None of these tendencies are new. What has changed is how fast our judgments travel. Digital platforms amplify moral outrage by making it effortless to express and rewarding it with likes and shares (Molly Crockett, 2017). In another research study, researchers analyzed Twitter conversations about politically charged issues and found that for every additional moral and emotional word in a post there was about a 20% increase in how widely it spread. Outrage is quick to spread but does so without the context (Brady and colleagues, 2017)!

The online disinhibition effect is the way a screen frees us to say what we would probably never say to someone’s face. It is much easier to judge and condemn a name than to sit across from a person and hear their story. And then… strangers join in! They offer confident judgments about the character, beliefs, and intentions of someone they have literally never met.

The Person on the Other Side of the Screen

But the truth is, a real person reads those comments, and the effects can go well beyond hurt feelings although I think hurting an actual person is enough of a reason to consider your words and actions. One survey found that 41% of American adults have experienced online harassment, which includes being purposely embarrassed (Vogels, 2021). A systematic review of research on adult victims found that most studies reported serious effects on mental health, including depression, anxiety, panic attacks, and suicidal ideation (Stevens et al., 2021). Public criticism is not always harassment, and not everyone who is criticized will suffer these outcomes, but the potential for harm still deserves to be taken seriously.

Think about what it is like to wake up and find strangers discussing your character, questioning your values, and urging others to stop supporting your work. Of course responding may make things worse, but its hard to stay silent and sometimes staying silent can look like an admission. And long after everyone else has moved on, the comments stay. Everything on line stays forever.

There is also so much we never even see. The person at the center of the negative comments may have just been diagnosed with cancer or perhaps they are grieving someone they loved, or caring for a sick parent, or quietly holding their life together through something no one else knows about. We see one sentence and not everything else someone is carrying while running a business or typing something in a rush. Public shaming lands on top of whatever a person is already living through because again, they are a real human being.

We don’t have to agree with someone, or even like them, to consider what our words, or posts, might do to their life.

Seeing the Whole Person

Imagine the worst thing you’ve ever said or something a few of thousands of people think about you for personal reasons, stripped of its context and handed to strangers who were asked to decide who you are. Would their verdict reflect your values, your relationships, or the people you’ve helped? Probably not. One moment may tell us something about a person, but it rarely tells us everything. The kinder and more accurate thing is to remember that every person and situation we judge has a whole life we cannot see.

item.title: When Dialogue Feels Broken, Build Something Together
item.description:
Career

When Dialogue Feels Broken, Build Something Together

Shared work can change how we treat one another, even amid deep disagreement.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Rising polarization is straining communities and making dialogue more difficult.
  • Small shared successes help build trust and keep people engaged over time.
  • Common goals can unite people across differences without requiring agreement.

This month, NBC News reported that 41% of American local officials surveyed said polarization was having “substantial negative effects” on their communities—roughly ten percentage points higher than in three previous surveys. Local officials described angry calls over fuel prices, bitter school board disputes over books, and, in one case, even threats against a council member seeking funds for emergency and homeless services.

We all know that political suspicion can consume the work of governing. Yet it also undermines the basic fabric of belonging--our confidence that we can be heard, that we can contribute, and ultimately count on one another.

In the face of extreme polarization, there’s a prescription we often hear: listen. Seek to understand other perspectives and look for common ground. While all of this is essential, there's a deeper level to consider.

When people struggle to trust one another’s intentions, even an invitation to dialogue can feel futile or suspect.

Psychology research points to a less-recognized but crucial way forward. Evidence shows that cooperating on even extremely simple shared tasks can improve how people treat one another, including when broader attitudes remain largely unchanged.

Crucially, we can begin improving a relationship before we’ve resolved how we feel about the person on the other side.

Action before agreement

In Mexico, an experiment involving more than 2,000 people paired political opponents for online tasks, including giving feedback on pop culture questions. Those assigned to collaborate as equals showed more tolerant behaviour toward people with opposing views three weeks later, without a clear change in broader political feelings. The measures included willingness to join a future discussion with political opponents.

In Iraq, researchers randomly assigned displaced Christians to soccer teams with either Christian or Muslim teammates. Christians who played alongside Muslims became more willing to join mixed teams and were more likely to train with Muslims six months later. They didn't suddenly change their entire view of the other group; what changed first was what they were willing to do together.

Of course, cooperation doesn’t replace justice, accountability, or confronting real abuses of power. Yet it offers a way to improve relationships where people can participate freely and meaningfully. It’s a place to start.

Trust can begin with a small commitment

Trust can feel like an enormous demand when we disagree deeply with somebody. But the key point is it can begin with a much more specific kind of judgment: “I can rely on you for this.”

Someone brings the supplies they promised or stays to finish the job. Their political identity hasn’t disappeared, but it is no longer the only thing we know about them.

A review of 137 cases of collaborative governance identified a recurring pattern: small wins can deepen trust and commitment, helping people continue working together. This finding draws on experience across many cases, rather than a controlled experiment.

The key is repeated interaction over time. One good encounter may be dismissed as an exception. When someone follows through again and again, we have more evidence to consider—and a shared history to draw on.
This is an important way to build belonging. People begin to expect one another’s presence, ask for help, and notice when someone is missing. Each person has a place in a relationship that continues.

Different interests can sustain common work

In the face of growing wildfire risks, there’s an opportunity for people to come together across differences. In a fire-prone area of Oregon, the Harney County Wildfire Collaborative brings together largely conservative ranchers along with environmentalists, tribal members, scientists, and government agencies. A phase of the wider project completed in 2025 removed overgrown juniper across more than 1,100 acres—a tangible result of sustained cooperation that reduced fire risk.

People can recognize the same need—like preventing a natural disaster, supporting children, helping neighbours after a storm—while disagreeing on broader political or scientific questions. Those different experiences can become useful to the work. One person knows the neighbourhood, another can organize transportation logistics, another can make machinery repairs.

Belonging grows when people have a useful role, real “voice and choice” in what happens, and the experience of having their contribution taken seriously.

A practical way to begin

Start with a priority that genuinely constitutes common ground. Choose a need everyone already cares about. “Would you help us get the school’s book swap ready?” “Can we develop a shared plan for flood readiness in the neighbourhood?” The task should be worthwhile and have intrinsic value even if nobody changes their politics as a result of its completion.

Participate as equals. Share decisions and responsibility, giving everyone room to influence the work. Make the first commitment achievable. That means agreeing on a manageable task, finishing it, and acknowledging what each person contributed.

Then do it again. Each occasion gives people a chance to build a record of reliability—and perhaps to have conversations that once felt impossible in an age of deep divisions.

Schools, libraries, faith communities, and sports clubs can facilitate these opportunities. The key message isn’t just that we can get work done, but also something more fundamental to belonging—you have something to contribute here.

This is reason for hope amid so much polarization. We can disagree profoundly and still learn, through experience, that we can rely on one another. Common work gives us something to accomplish. Shared wins give us reasons to trust. Over time, those experiences can help us recover something rare and precious in divided times like these: the confidence that, despite our differences, we can still show up for one another.

item.title: Narcissism and the Aesthetics of Grandiosity
item.description:
Narcissism

Narcissism and the Aesthetics of Grandiosity

From Roman altars to annual reports, the narcissistic ego wants to be seen.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Grandiosity, a central feature of narcissism, tends to leave a visible mark on what powerful people build.
  • Narcissism predicts who emerges as a leader, though not who leads well.
  • Strangers can read narcissism from a photograph with modest accuracy, mostly from cues of visible effort.
  • Monuments tend to outlive the egos that ordered them and carry meanings their patrons never intended.

The Roman emperor Augustus presided over a series of structures that bore his name, from the Forum of Augustus to the Ara Pacis Augustae (the Altar of Augustan Peace), which the Senate commissioned in his honor in 13 BC and which stood in the same district as his own mausoleum. Augustus’ self-reference was not subtle. The mausoleum’s visual proximity to the Altar of Peace, a monument designed to represent the grandeur of the Roman Empire, immortalized Augustus’ memory as inextricable from the civilization itself.

Source: Osviel Rodriguez Valdés/Pexels

Grandiosity of this magnitude is not unique to Augustus or Mussolini, who famously excavated the Ara Pacis and reassembled it beside the mausoleum in 1938 to evoke the same Italian nationalistic pride as his predecessor almost 2,000 years before. Grandiosity by itself does not warrant a diagnosis of narcissism, but it is one of the most salient features of the personality disorder. The erection of monuments in the name of the great leader shows, with striking regularity across history and continents, that narcissism is legible in aesthetics. The Romans wouldn’t have called Augustus’ self-preoccupation narcissistic. However, they may have whispered to each other in the forum about his superbia (arrogance and self-importance) and rampant philautia, a Greek term denoting self-love in both its healthy and destructive forms.

Having studied the effects of narcissism on the psyche and relationships, I’m familiar with how narcissistic personality traits can find their way into many areas of life. However, as I’ve delved into the psychology of aesthetics, I’ve realized that grandiosity, in particular, is evident in the very structures narcissists choose to represent their egos. This shows up in everything from their physical presentation and image curation to the buildings, monuments, and altars that bear their names. Each construction in the physical world reflects an inner self that cannot fully feel its own importance without others' excessive admiration. A building, statue, or triumphal arch carved from stone or marble and inscribed with the leader’s name and, in some cases, like the Ara Pacis, their image, more closely matches their inner experience.

Having narcissistic traits does not always indicate that someone will seek leadership positions, and not all leaders are narcissistic. However, researchers have found that narcissism predicts who will emerge as a leader, largely because narcissists tend to display more extroversion (Grijalva et al., 2015). Narcissism also doesn’t positively correlate with good leadership, though narcissistic leaders tend to rate themselves as more effective than their colleagues do, convinced that they are, in fact, the only person for the job.

Confidence is attractive to many people, and the narcissist has confidence in spades. But in the case of leaders like Julius Caesar, Mussolini, Hitler, and Napoleon, history shows that grandiosity existed alongside a voracious need for empire expansion at any cost. The desire to conquer and literally mark the land with reminders of their impact through architecture and aesthetic modeling speaks to existing research: Grandiosity tends to predict who will climb to the top of the ladder. That said, many self-important people never reach notoriety worthy of architectural immortalization, but the grandiose among them will strive for it nonetheless.

Aesthetic narcissism is expressed on a spectrum, from subtle to glaring. In a 2008 study, Vazire and colleagues photographed 160 people against a blank wall and had seven observers rate each person’s narcissism from the photograph alone. Their ratings tracked participants’ actual narcissism scores about as well as those of friends who knew them. Women higher in narcissism tended to wear more makeup, men who wore glasses tended to score lower, and overall the clearest cues were expensive, stylish clothing and an appearance that took evident effort.

Similarly, since Chatterjee and Hambrick (2007) couldn’t hand CEOs narcissism inventories, they estimated narcissism from observable traits, including how prominently each CEO’s photograph appeared in the company’s annual report. CEOs who scored high took greater risks in business and, as a result, had bigger wins and bigger losses than those who didn’t, likely because of greater grandiosity. Later researchers have questioned how well these observed traits capture narcissism (Koch-Bayram & Biemann, 2020), although it’s telling that one of the first places they looked was the size of a leader’s own image.

For most narcissistic people, a leadership position, polished exterior, or prominent photograph must suffice to quell the ego’s need for external admiration. But for the most grandiose among them, only the largest and most impressive trophies will do. For the authoritarians and imperialists among them, their kingdoms reflected their ambition in no uncertain terms.

On its face, the architectural grandeur of the Republic was impersonal: stone and marble meant to outlive the one who commissioned it, without reflecting the leader’s vainglory. Imperialism reverses the calculation, so that the design itself is a direct reflection of the ego that envisioned it. Imperial projects tell a story of Herculean egoic breadth, with workforces and material costs to match the idealized vision of a capital built on the leader’s name.

The Arc de Triomphe is instructive on this point. Commissioned in 1806 by Napoleon to celebrate his victory at Austerlitz, the arch took 30 years to complete. However, since 1923, veterans have rekindled the eternal flame of the Unknown Soldier there each evening, without mentioning Napoleon. Despite the grandiose intentions behind their construction, monuments outlive the egos they were meant to memorialize and begin carrying meanings their patrons never intended. Some monuments are destroyed precisely because the people who inspired them are so dubious that only erasing them can cleanse the stains they left behind. This shows that institutions can outlast individual personalities, remaining resilient despite, and sometimes because of, the grandiose leaders who inspired them.

Whether it’s made visible through makeup, an impeccable wardrobe with all the right labels, a large glossy photograph in an annual report, an ornate mausoleum, or a triumphal arch, narcissism is legible in the physical world. Even without the psychological content that inspired the form, something in us recognizes superbia and philautia in our bosses, neighbors, favorite influencers, and politicians.
